decks.domain: Bicyclists, motorcyclists, pedestrians and distracted driving

cards.front: Why must you not block a bike lane, and when may you cross one?
cards.back: Blocking a bike lane pushes bicyclists into the main travel lane and can endanger them; you may cross a bike lane only when turning or entering or leaving a road, driveway or alley.

cards.front: What is the difference between crossing a bike lane and blocking it?
cards.back: You may cross a bike lane to turn or to enter or leave a road, driveway or alley, but you may not block it.

cards.front: Must bicyclists stay in the bike lane, and where may they ride on a one-way multi-lane street?
cards.back: People on bikes are allowed to ride outside a bike lane, and on a multi-lane one-way street they may ride on either the right or the left side.

cards.front: What does Colorado's stop-as-yield law let some bicyclists do?
cards.back: Under a law passed in two thousand twenty-two, bicyclists aged fifteen and older who already have the right-of-way at a clear intersection may treat stop signs as yield signs and red stop lights as stop signs.

cards.front: Which bicyclists does the stop-as-yield rule cover, and when?
cards.back: The stop-as-yield rule covers bicyclists aged fifteen and up only, and only when the intersection is clear and they already have the right-of-way.

cards.front: Which direction must bicyclists ride, and where should you still look for them?
cards.back: Bicyclists must ride in the same direction as traffic, but look for them anywhere on the roadway anyway.

decks.domain: Bicyclists, motorcyclists, pedestrians and distracted driving

cards.front: When should your turn signal be on?
cards.back: Always signal before turning and keep the signal off while going straight.

cards.front: How should you make a right turn near bicyclists?
cards.back: Turn right hugging the curb, using a Conflict Zone where one is marked, so riders approaching from behind are not tempted to pass you on the right.

cards.front: A bicyclist is beside you as you prepare to turn right. What do you do?
cards.back: When a bicyclist is beside you as you prepare to turn right, slow down, yield and let the rider clear the intersection first.

cards.front: What must you do before a legal right turn on red?
cards.back: Before a legal right turn on red, stop completely and look for bicyclists behind or beside you, turning left from across the street, or riding in the lane you will join.

cards.front: When must you check your path and blind spots for bicyclists?
cards.back: Check your path and blind spots for bicyclists before backing, changing lanes or turning, and before a left turn look for riders on the right side or shoulder and judge their speed.

decks.domain: Bicyclists, motorcyclists, pedestrians and distracted driving

cards.front: What is forcing a bicyclist off the road considered?
cards.back: Forcing a bicyclist off the road counts as aggressive driving and carries legal consequences.

cards.front: How should you think of bicyclists on the road?
cards.back: Treat bicyclists as drivers with a right to the road who are also more vulnerable, look for them actively and judge their speed and distance carefully.

cards.front: When should you give a bicyclist more than three feet?
cards.back: Give a bicyclist more than three feet of room when you drive a bigger vehicle, are on a rural road or face wind, because wind blasts are dangerous.

cards.front: Why should you never stop suddenly in front of a bicyclist?
cards.back: Never turn sharply, slow down or stop suddenly in front of a bicyclist, because car brakes are stronger than bicycle brakes and a crash could follow.

cards.front: How do wet roads and debris affect bicyclists?
cards.back: Wet roads and debris affect bicyclists far more than drivers, so take extra care around riders in those conditions.

cards.front: When may you honk near bicyclists?
cards.back: Do not honk near bicyclists unless a crash is about to happen, because the noise can startle them into crashing.

decks.domain: Bicyclists, motorcyclists, pedestrians and distracted driving

cards.front: What is the Dutch Reach?
cards.back: Before opening a door when parked on the street, check sides and rear for bicyclists and open it with the hand nearer the center of the vehicle, a habit called the Dutch Reach.

cards.front: Why might a bicyclist not hand-signal, and what clues should you watch for?
cards.back: Bicyclists must hand-signal turns and stops but may be unable to when their skill or road conditions require both hands on the handlebars, so watch for head turns or shoulder checks as clues.

cards.front: What are the bicycle hand signals for turns and stopping?
cards.back: A bicyclist signals a right turn with the right arm straight out or the left arm bent upward at a right angle, a left turn with the left arm straight out, and slowing or stopping with the left arm bent downward.

cards.front: What does a bicyclist's raised, bent left arm mean?
cards.back: A bicyclist has two valid right-turn signals, right arm straight out or left arm bent up, so a raised left arm means right, not left.

cards.front: How does a downward left arm differ from a straight left arm?
cards.back: A left arm bent downward means the rider is slowing or stopping, while a left arm held straight out means a left turn.

decks.domain: Bicyclists, motorcyclists, pedestrians and distracted driving

cards.front: What rights do motorcyclists have, and why are they at risk?
cards.back: Motorcyclists have the same rights and duties as other drivers but little crash protection, so a hit from a larger vehicle can injure or kill them.

cards.front: How much of the lane is a motorcycle entitled to, and why might it shift?
cards.back: Motorcycles are entitled to a full lane width and often shift within it to see, be seen and avoid hazards, and strong wind can push one out of its lane.

cards.front: When may a motorcycle lane filter?
cards.back: A two-wheeled motorcycle may lane filter past a stopped vehicle in its lane only when neighboring lanes are also stopped, there is room, and it moves no faster than fifteen miles per hour.

cards.front: What is lane filtering, and which vehicles is it written for?
cards.back: Lane filtering is passing stopped traffic within a lane at low speed, and the rule is written for two-wheeled motorcycles.

cards.front: Why do motorcycles call for extra caution and a longer following distance?
cards.back: Motorcycles are small and hard to see, can speed up and stop faster than expected, and are endangered by road defects and debris, so use extra caution and a longer following distance.

decks.domain: Bicyclists, motorcyclists, pedestrians and distracted driving

cards.front: What is one common bicycle collision, and how do you prevent it?
cards.back: Common bicycle collisions include a driver turning left in front of an oncoming rider, so look for riders on the shoulder or lane edge before turning.

cards.front: What other collisions with bicyclists are common?
cards.back: Other common bicycle collisions come from running stop signs or signals, opening a door without looking back, riders going the wrong way against traffic, and drivers pulling out of driveways without looking.

cards.front: Is sharing the road just a safety habit?
cards.back: Sharing the road is required by law, not just a safety habit.

decks.domain: Bicyclists, motorcyclists, pedestrians and distracted driving

cards.front: Who counts as a pedestrian, and whose duty is it to watch for them?
cards.back: Pedestrians, meaning people standing, walking, running or using mobility aids on public roads or private property, are the most vulnerable road users, and watching out for them is the driver's duty.

cards.front: Why may you need to drive slower than the limit near pedestrians?
cards.back: Obey the speed limit or go slower when needed to spot and react to pedestrians, and remember that children and wheelchair users sit lower and are harder to see.

cards.front: Where do pedestrians have the right of way?
cards.back: Pedestrians have the right-of-way at every intersection and crosswalk, painted or not, and drivers must yield or stop completely to let them cross safely.

cards.front: Do pedestrians have the right of way where no crosswalk lines are painted?
cards.back: Pedestrians have the right-of-way at intersections and crosswalks even where no lines are painted.

cards.front: What must you do for pedestrians before turning on red?
cards.back: When turning on red, be in the correct lane, stop completely and check for pedestrians in all directions before creeping forward to look for traffic.

cards.front: In what order do you check before turning on red?
cards.back: When turning on red, the checks come in order: stop and check for pedestrians in every direction first, then edge forward to look for vehicles.

cards.front: Where must you never stop at a crosswalk, and why never pass a stopped vehicle there?
cards.back: Never stop with any part of your vehicle over the crosswalk, and never pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk, since its driver may be waiting for a pedestrian you cannot see.

cards.front: Where should you take special care for pedestrians?
cards.back: Watch for people getting in or out of parked cars, drive very carefully near schools, parks, parking lots, bus stops and events, and check mirrors and blind spots when backing out.

decks.domain: Bicyclists, motorcyclists, pedestrians and distracted driving

cards.front: What counts as a distraction while driving?
cards.back: A distraction is anything that takes your eyes, hands or mind off driving, and mental distractions are just as dangerous as physical ones; even tuning the radio is risky in bad weather or heavy traffic.

cards.front: Which activities should you avoid while driving?
cards.back: Do not eat, drink, read, smoke, vape, apply makeup or adjust music while driving.

cards.front: How do alcohol and drugs change the danger of a distraction?
cards.back: Alcohol, marijuana and many other drugs reduce the ability to handle several tasks, so a distraction that is merely hazardous for a sober driver can be deadly for an impaired one.

cards.front: When may drivers use a mobile electronic device, and what can careless use bring?
cards.back: Drivers may not use a mobile electronic device unless hands-free or in an emergency; careless driving caused by texting or other manual device use can bring a fine or a misdemeanor charge, so pull off the road to use a phone.

cards.front: Does hands-free use protect you from a careless driving charge?
cards.back: Hands-free use is allowed for mobile devices, but careless driving from texting or any manual device use can still bring a fine or misdemeanor charge.

cards.front: How can you prevent distraction before you drive?
cards.back: To prevent distraction, skip phone use and emotional conversations, restrain children properly, put pets in a carrier or kennel, learn your controls, preset radio stations and playlists, and plan your route before driving.

cards.front: What is aggressive driving?
cards.back: Aggressive driving is any willful behavior behind the wheel that endangers people or property without regard for safety.

recap_hooks.text: Cross bike lanes only to turn or enter or leave a road, never block them, and remember riders go with traffic.
Turn right close to the curb and let a rider beside you clear first.
Never force a rider off the road, never stop suddenly in front of one, and honk only to prevent a crash.
Open doors with the Dutch Reach, and read a raised left arm as a right turn.
Motorcycles get a full lane, may filter only past stopped traffic, and need a longer following distance.
Most collisions with riders come from left turns, signals, doors, wrong-way riding and driveways.
Pedestrians have the right of way at every crosswalk, painted or not; on red, check for walkers first.
Distraction takes your eyes, hands or mind off driving; use phones only hands-free or after pulling over.
